fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Peter says, "But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed." (1 Peter 3:14) Suffering and blessing in the same sentence is a lot to chew on, but that's what the text says. And Peter wrote it to people he calls "exiles" (1 Peter 1:1).

Not quite, friend. The verse says, "But respond with gentleness and respect…" (1 Peter 3:15) So Peter wants the answer given with gentleness and respect, not swung like a rolling pin. The way you say it counts too.

Louder? I think that's me on a Monday morning, not what Peter says. The verse says those who slander the believers "…may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ." (1 Peter 3:16) Good behavior is what does the work there.

That's the one. Peter says, "For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." (1 Peter 3:18) Once. Not a repeat, not a second round. One time, and Peter says it was for the unrighteous.
Three is a nice number, but it's not the one here. Peter says Christ "…suffered for sins once for all…" (1 Peter 3:18) That's once. A second round isn't in the verse, and neither is a third.

Yep. Peter says God "…waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." (1 Peter 3:20) Noah is the man God told to build the ark (Genesis 6:14). God's patience is right there in the text.

Moses is a big name, so I see the pull. He's the one who led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10). But Peter says God "…waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." (1 Peter 3:20) Noah is the one tied to the ark here.

Elijah is a fine guess, since he was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36). But Peter says God "…waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." (1 Peter 3:20) The ark points straight to Noah.

Passover, huh? I get it, that's a big one. I once tried stamping a cookie with the wrong stamper, and it came out looking like a different cookie entirely. Peter says, "And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also…" (1 Peter 3:21) Baptism is the word that fits the blank.

Sabbath! Good word, friend, but wrong cookie cutter for this blank. Peter says, "And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also…" (1 Peter 3:21) The water of Noah's day points to baptism, so that's what goes in the blank.

A record of good works sounds official, like a stack of paperwork. But Peter calls baptism "…the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) He doesn't call it a record of good works. The conscience is the focus.

That's right. Peter says Jesus "…has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him." (1 Peter 3:22) Angels, authorities and powers are all subject to Him. That's a good place to end the passage.

I see the thought, but that isn't what this verse says. Peter says Jesus is at God's right hand "…with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him." (1 Peter 3:22) Subject to Him is the wording. Standing against Him isn't in the verse.
